fathers/boethius/summary: Roman aristocrat, consul and minister of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, who translated Aristotle’s logic, wrote theological tractates defining ‘person’ and ‘nature’, and composed the Consolation of Philosophy while awaiting execution.
fathers/boethius/story:
Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius was born around 477 into the great Anician family and raised after his father’s death by the senator Symmachus, whose daughter Rusticiana he married. Extraordinarily learned in Greek — some scholars think he studied in Alexandria or Athens, though this is uncertain — he set himself to translate into Latin and comment on all of Plato and Aristotle and to show their agreement. He completed only Aristotle’s logical works and Porphyry’s Isagoge, together with handbooks on arithmetic and music; these became the core of Western logical education until the twelfth century.

Boethius rose high in the service of Theodoric, the Arian Ostrogothic king of Italy: consul in 510, he saw his two sons made joint consuls in 522, and in the same year became magister officiorum. But in 523, amid tensions between Theodoric and Constantinople, he defended the senator Albinus against a charge of treasonable correspondence with the emperor, was himself accused, condemned without a proper hearing and imprisoned near Pavia. He was executed in 524 (some date it 525).

His five theological tractates (Opuscula sacra) applied Aristotelian logic to Christian doctrine. On the Trinity explains how ‘God’ is predicated of Father, Son and Spirit without plurality; Against Eutyches and Nestorius gives the classic definition of a person as ‘an individual substance of a rational nature’ (naturae rationabilis individua substantia); and the treatise later known as De hebdomadibus distinguishes being (esse) from that which is (id quod est). The discovery in 1877 of a fragment of Cassiodorus (the Anecdoton Holderi) confirmed that he wrote theological works.

In prison he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, a prosimetrum in which Lady Philosophy leads the prisoner from complaint against Fortune to understanding of providence, the true good and the compatibility of divine foreknowledge with human freedom — God sees all time in one eternal present. Remarkably, the book never mentions Christ, which has led some to question his Christianity; most scholars see it as a deliberate philosophical exercise by a Christian working within reason alone.

The Consolation was among the most widely read books of the Middle Ages, translated by Alfred the Great, Notker, Jean de Meun, Chaucer and Elizabeth I. Boethius was venerated at Pavia as a martyr for orthodoxy against an Arian king, buried in San Pietro in Ciel d’Oro near Augustine’s relics; his local cult was confirmed in 1883.
fathers/boethius/roots/0/text: The Consolation’s ascent to the Good and its account of eternity draw on Proclus and the Alexandrian commentators (Ammonius).
fathers/boethius/roots/1/text: Translated and commented on the Organon and Porphyry’s Isagoge, transmitting Aristotelian logic to the Latin West.
fathers/boethius/roots/2/text: Hymn ‘O qui perpetua’ (Consolation III m. 9) paraphrases Plato’s Timaeus; he aimed to show Plato and Aristotle in harmony.
fathers/boethius/roots/3/text: The Consolation’s early books use Stoic consolation literature on Fortune and the indifference of external goods.
fathers/boethius/roots/4/text: His De Trinitate explicitly follows Augustine’s ‘seeds of reasoning’ on the Trinity.
fathers/boethius/keyTeachings/0: A person is ‘an individual substance of a rational nature’.
fathers/boethius/keyTeachings/1: God’s eternity is ‘the complete, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life’, so divine foreknowledge does not impose necessity.
fathers/boethius/keyTeachings/2: True happiness is God himself, the highest good, not Fortune’s gifts.
fathers/boethius/keyTeachings/3: Evil is powerless and in a sense nothing; the wicked are punished by their own wickedness.
fathers/boethius/keyTeachings/4: Faith and reason should be joined: ‘as far as you are able, join faith to reason’.
fathers/boethius/works/0/note: Prosimetrum on Fortune, the good, providence and freedom; written in prison.
fathers/boethius/works/1/note: Five short works including De Trinitate and Contra Eutychen et Nestorium.
fathers/boethius/works/2/title: Translations and commentaries on Aristotle’s logic and Porphyry’s Isagoge
fathers/boethius/works/2/note: Including two commentaries on the Isagoge that posed the medieval problem of universals.
fathers/boethius/works/3/title: De institutione arithmetica and De institutione musica
fathers/boethius/works/3/note: Handbooks of the quadrivium, a term he coined.
fathers/boethius/doctrineContributions/0: Gave Latin theology precise definitions of person, nature and substance used by all later scholastics.
fathers/boethius/doctrineContributions/1: His treatise against Eutyches and Nestorius applied Chalcedonian categories with logical rigour.
fathers/boethius/doctrineContributions/2: The Consolation’s reconciliation of providence, foreknowledge and free will became the standard medieval treatment.
fathers/boethius/doctrineContributions/3: Established the use of Aristotelian logic as a tool of theology, preparing scholastic method.
fathers/boethius/laterInfluence/0/text: Called ‘the last of the Romans, the first of the scholastics’; Gilbert of Poitiers, Aquinas and others commented on his tractates.
fathers/boethius/laterInfluence/1/text: The Consolation shaped Alfred, Dante (who places him in Paradise), Chaucer’s Troilus and The Knight’s Tale, and Elizabeth I.
fathers/boethius/laterInfluence/2/text: His Isagoge commentary launched the medieval debate on universals; his definition of eternity remains central in philosophy of religion.
fathers/boethius/laterInfluence/3/text: Valued as a model of Christian humanism; his definition of person is still debated in Trinitarian theology.
fathers/boethius/reception/0/text: Venerated locally at Pavia as St Severinus Boethius, a martyr; cultus confirmed by the Congregation of Rites in 1883 (feast 23 October).
fathers/boethius/reception/1/text: Little known in Byzantium until Maximos Planudes translated the Consolation into Greek (c. 1300).
fathers/boethius/reception/2/text: Admired as a philosopher and literary classic; translated by Elizabeth I and read in Protestant schools.
fathers/boethius/reception/3/text: Studied as a transmitter of ancient logic and as a philosopher in his own right.
fathers/boethius/controversies/0: Whether the Consolation, silent on Christ, shows a philosopher whose Christianity was nominal; most scholars reject this reading.
fathers/boethius/controversies/1: Whether his execution was political (treason) or religious (Catholic against an Arian king); the later martyr cult stressed the latter.
fathers/boethius/controversies/2: Authorship of De fide catholica among the tractates is debated.
fathers/boethius/quote/text: Eternity is the complete, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/summary: Anonymous author of c. 500 who wrote as Dionysius, Paul’s Athenian convert (Acts 17:34), fusing Proclus’ Neoplatonism with Christian liturgy and Scripture; his apophatic and hierarchical theology profoundly shaped Eastern and Western mysticism.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/story:
The corpus attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite — The Divine Names, The Mystical Theology, The Celestial Hierarchy, The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy and ten Letters — presents itself as the work of the Athenian judge converted by Paul’s speech on the Areopagus (Acts 17:34), addressed to Timothy and mentioning the eclipse at the crucifixion. The texts first surface in the 510s–520s, cited by the miaphysite Severus of Antioch; at a colloquy in Constantinople in 532 Hypatius of Ephesus doubted their authenticity, but they were soon accepted as apostolic.

Modern scholarship rests on the discovery, made independently by Hugo Koch and Josef Stiglmayr in 1895, that Dionysius’ treatment of evil in Divine Names 4 reproduces Proclus’ On the Existence of Evils. The author therefore wrote after Proclus (d. 485), probably in Syria around 500, perhaps a monk sympathetic to the Christology of the Henotikon. Identifications with Peter the Iberian, Severus or the last Athenian scholarch Damascius have been proposed; none is established.

Dionysius describes a universe of light flowing out from the superessential Godhead (thearchy) and drawing all things back to union through ordered ranks. He coined the word ‘hierarchy’: nine choirs of angels in three triads, and a church hierarchy of bishop, priest and deacon, monks, laity and catechumens, mediating purification, illumination and perfection. The liturgy — baptism, eucharist (synaxis), chrismation, ordination, monastic tonsure and funeral — is interpreted as an icon of this cosmic movement.

His most influential pages concern the names of God. Affirmative theology (cataphatic) praises God by all the names of Scripture; negative theology (apophatic) denies them all, since God is beyond being; and the soul finally passes, like Moses into the cloud on Sinai, into the ‘brilliant darkness’ of union beyond knowing. This programme gave Christian mysticism its classic vocabulary.

Through John of Scythopolis’ scholia (c. 540) and Maximus the Confessor’s defence, the corpus became authoritative in Byzantium. In the West it was translated by Hilduin (c. 832) and John Scotus Eriugena (c. 862), confused with Denis, martyr-bishop of Paris, and commented on by Hugh of St Victor, Albert, Bonaventure and Aquinas, who cites him some 1,700 times. Lorenzo Valla and Erasmus questioned its authorship; Luther judged him ‘more a Platonist than a Christian’.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/roots/0/text: Dependent on Proclus and Iamblichus for procession and return, triadic structure, theurgy and the treatment of evil as privation.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/roots/1/text: Draws on Gregory of Nyssa’s Life of Moses (ascent into the divine darkness) and the Cappadocian doctrine of God’s incomprehensibility.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/roots/2/text: Builds his doctrine of divine names on biblical titles of God and interprets Sinai, the seraphim of Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel’s visions.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/roots/3/text: Claims the authority of Paul’s convert; the pseudonym itself bound pagan wisdom to apostolic origins.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/roots/4/text: Writes probably from Syrian monastic circles and gives monks a defined rank in the ecclesiastical hierarchy.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/keyTeachings/0: God is ‘beyond being’ (hyperousios), known supremely by unknowing.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/keyTeachings/1: Cataphatic and apophatic theology: affirm every name of God, then deny them all.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/keyTeachings/2: Hierarchy as a sacred order that mediates purification, illumination and perfection.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/keyTeachings/3: Nine choirs of angels in three triads (seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, powers, authorities; principalities, archangels, angels).
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/keyTeachings/4: Evil is not a substance but a privation of good.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/keyTeachings/5: Union (henosis) with God and deification as the goal of creation.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/works/0/note: On the biblical names of God: Good, Being, Life, Wisdom, Power, One.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/works/1/note: Short treatise on ascent into the darkness of unknowing; foundation of apophatic mysticism.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/works/2/note: Nine angelic orders in three triads; source of medieval angelology.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/works/3/note: Mystagogical interpretation of the sacraments and orders of the church.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/works/4/note: Includes letters to ‘Timothy’ and ‘John the Evangelist’ on Patmos.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/doctrineContrib: Gave Christian mysticism its vocabulary of apophasis, divine darkness and union.
His nine-fold angelic hierarchy became standard in East and West, from Gregory the Great to Dante.
Developed apophatic theology of the divine names, later decisive for the essence–energies distinction and for Aquinas’ analogy.
His mystagogy shaped Byzantine liturgical commentary and Western sacramental symbolism.
Classic Christian statement of evil as privation within a procession–return cosmology.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/laterInfluence/: Maximus the Confessor, John of Damascus and Gregory Palamas all treated him as an apostolic authority.
Through Eriugena, the Victorines, Bonaventure and Aquinas, he shaped scholastic theology, Gothic light-theology (Suger of Saint-Denis) and the Cloud of Unknowing.
Valla and Erasmus exposed the pseudonym; Luther rejected his speculative mysticism; Calvin dismissed his angelology as idle speculation.
Revived by Lossky, Balthasar, Marion and Denys Turner as a resource for negative theology and post-modern thought.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/reception/0/tex: Honoured under the name of the Areopagite (feast 3 October); his writings are treated as patristic authority whatever their date.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/reception/1/tex: Highly influential on scholasticism; modern Catholic scholarship accepts the pseudonymity while valuing the corpus.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/reception/2/tex: First cited by Severus of Antioch and translated into Syriac by Sergius of Resh‘aina (d. 536); valued in the Syriac tradition.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/reception/3/tex: Luther and many Protestants saw him as a channel of Platonism into the gospel; some modern Protestants have rediscovered his apophaticism.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/controversies/0: The pseudonym: a sixth-century author claiming apostolic authority, exposed by Renaissance philology and by Koch and Stiglmayr in 1895.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/controversies/1: How far his theology is Christian rather than Proclean — critics note how rarely he discusses the cross; defenders stress the centrality of Christ in the liturgy and Letter 4.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/controversies/2: His Christology (‘a new theandric energy’, Letter 4) was claimed by both miaphysites and Monothelites before Maximus interpreted it in a Chalcedonian sense.
fathers/pseudo-dionysius/quote/text: Leave behind the senses and the operations of the intellect … and, to the extent possible, strive upward unknowingly toward union with him who is beyond all being and knowledge.
